title: Electromagnetic Induction
short_intro: Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon of generating an electromotive force (emf) in a circuit by changing the magnetic flux linked with it. It forms the foundational principle underlying electrical generators, transformers, and inductors.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Faraday's laws of induction, Lenz's law, motional emf, self-induction, and mutual induction.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Differential and integral forms of Maxwell's equations relating to electromagnetic induction, betatron principle, eddy currents, and time-varying magnetic fields generating non-conservative electric fields.

prerequisites: Lorentz force and magnetic force on moving charges

concept_notes.heading: Faraday's Laws of Electromagnetic Induction
bullets: First Law: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a closed circuit changes, an electromotive force (emf) is induced in the circuit, which lasts only as long as the change in magnetic flux continues.
Second Law: The magnitude of the induced emf is directly proportional to the time rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit.
Magnetic flux is defined as the scalar product of the magnetic field vector and the area vector, given by Φ = B · A = BA cosθ.

concept_notes.heading: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
bullets: Lenz's Law states that the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to oppose the very cause (change in magnetic flux) that produces it.
Mathematically, this opposition is incorporated as a negative sign in Faraday's law: e = - (dΦ / dt).
Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of energy; mechanical work done in moving a conductor against a magnetic force is converted into electrical energy.

concept_notes.heading: Motional Electromotive Force
bullets: When a conductor of length l moves with a velocity v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B, a potential difference is induced across its ends.
The free electrons inside the conductor experience a magnetic Lorentz force (F = q(v × B)), causing them to accumulate at one end until an electrostatic field balances the magnetic force.
The resulting motional emf is given by e = Blv when velocity, magnetic field, and length are mutually perpendicular.

concept_notes.heading: Self-Induction and Mutual Induction
bullets: Self-induction is the property of a coil by virtue of which it opposes any change in the strength of current flowing through it by inducing an emf within itself.
The self-induced emf depends on the self-inductance L, such that e = - L (di / dt).
Mutual induction is the phenomenon where a change in current in a primary coil induces an emf in a nearby secondary coil, quantified by the mutual inductance M.

derivations.title: Motional Electromotive Force in a Conducting Rod
derivations.conditions: A straight conducting rod of length l moving with constant velocity v in a uniform perpendicular magnetic field B.
steps: Consider a charge q inside the rod moving with velocity v in magnetic field B. The magnetic force on the charge is F_m = qvB.
This force drives charges toward one end, establishing an electric field E inside the rod such that the electrostatic force F_e = qE balances the magnetic force at equilibrium.
Equating magnitudes: qE = qvB, which gives the internal electric field E = vB.
The induced emf e is the line integral of the electric field along the length l of the rod: e = ∫ E dl = E l = Blv.

derivations.title: Energy Stored in an Inductor
derivations.conditions: A current i is established in an inductor of self-inductance L against the back emf.
steps: The instantaneous back emf opposing the growth of current is e = L (di / dt).
The rate at which work must be done by an external source to drive the current against this back emf is P = - ie = i L (di / dt).
The total work W done in increasing the current from 0 to I is obtained by integrating the power over time: W = ∫ P dt = ∫ L i di from 0 to I.
Performing the integration yields W = \frac{1}{2} LI^2.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnet and Coil Relative Motion (Faraday's Experiment)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bar magnet moving toward a stationary closed loop connected to a zero-center galvanometer, showing deflection.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Approaching the north pole deflects the galvanometer in one direction, while receding deflects it oppositely, confirming directional dependence of induced emf (Lenz's law).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT to check polarity prediction and direction of induced current.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Growth of Current in an L-R Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An exponential growth curve of current i versus time t, starting from 0 and approaching a steady-state value I_0 = V/R with time constant \tau = L/R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The back emf slows down the immediate rise of current when a DC voltage is switched on, asymptotic to the maximum ohmic current.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT for time constant calculations and graphical interpretation of transient states.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Alternating Magnetic Flux and Induced emf Sine Wave
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Sinusoidal magnetic flux \Phi(t) = \Phi_0 \cos(\omega t) plotted alongside its derivative curve (induced emf) which is a sine wave shifted in phase.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that rate of change of a cosine flux wave produces a sine wave emf, leading by 90 degrees in phase.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Relates electromagnetic induction directly to AC generation principles in electrical machinery.

solved_numericals.question: A circular loop of radius 0.1 m is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T perpendicular to the plane of the loop. If the magnetic field is reduced to zero in 0.02 s, find the magnitude of the induced emf in the loop.
solution_steps: Calculate initial magnetic flux: \Phi_1 = B \cdot A = 0.5 \times \pi \times (0.1)^2 = 0.5 \times 3.1416 \times 0.01 = 0.0157 \text{ Wb}.
Apply Faraday's law magnitude formula: e = \frac{|\Phi_2 - \Phi_1|}{\Delta t} = \frac{0.0157 - 0}{0.02}.

solved_numericals.question: A metallic rod of length 0.5 m rotates with an angular velocity of 20 rad/s about an axis passing through one of its ends, perpendicular to the rod, inside a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T directed parallel to the axis of rotation. Wait, let's correct the geometry: magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of rotation. Calculate the induced emf across the ends of the rod.
solution_steps: Consider an element of the rod of length dr at a distance r from the axis of rotation.
The linear speed of this element is v = \omega r.
The elemental induced emf is de = B v dr = B \omega r dr.
Integrate from r = 0 to r = l: e = \int_0^l B \omega r dr = \frac{1}{2} B \omega l^2.
Substitute values: B = 0.4 T, \omega = 20 \text{ rad/s}, l = 0.5 \text{ m}.

solved_numericals.question: An inductor of self-inductance 5 H carries a steady current of 2 A. If the current is uniformly interrupted and drops to zero in 10 ms, calculate the average induced emf during this time interval.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 5 \text{ H}, \Delta i = 0 - 2 = -2 \text{ A}, \Delta t = 10 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s} = 0.01 \text{ s}.
Use the formula for self-induced emf: e = - L \frac{\Delta i}{\Delta t}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Faraday's law in the form e = - d\Phi/dt assumes that the path of integration is stationary in inertial frames, whereas moving media require the Lorentz force approach.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Induced emf requires a complete closed circuit to be generated.
common_misconceptions.correct: An induced emf is produced across the ends of a conductor whenever magnetic flux changes, regardless of whether the circuit is open or closed.
common_misconceptions.why: Current only flows if the circuit is closed, but the emf exists purely due to flux variation or conductor motion.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Lenz's law violates the conservation of energy because it opposes motion.
common_misconceptions.correct: Lenz's law is a direct enforcement of conservation of energy.
common_misconceptions.why: External mechanical work must be continuously performed to overcome magnetic braking forces, which directly supplies the electrical energy generated.

quick_revision: The negative sign in Faraday's law mathematically represents Lenz's law and energy conservation.
